vignette:
Tasi, at 48, carries the weight of years not just in the calloused strength of his hands from a lifetime of roofing, but in the heavy silence he keeps. He’s a man of the islands, robust and proud, with a quiet dignity that his family and community in the tight-knit Oceania diaspora have always respected. He’s been married to his wife, Lena, for twenty-five years, and together they’ve built a life around their children and the steady rhythm of his work. But lately, that rhythm has become a jarring discord.

It was three years ago, after a large commercial roofing job. The crew celebrated with drinks, a rare indulgence for Tasi, who usually prefers to be home with his family. He remembers the camaraderie, the laughter, and then a hazy blank. The next morning, he woke in an unfamiliar place, disoriented, his body aching in ways that weren't just from the liquor. A profound, sickening sense of violation washed over him. He knew, with an icy certainty that froze his blood, that something terrible had happened. He fled, scrubbing himself raw in the shower, trying to wash away the feeling, the memory, the shame. He never told Lena, never told anyone. How could he? A man, assaulted? The thought felt impossible, emasculating.

Initially, he tried to bury it. He threw himself into work, pushing his body harder on the roofs, hoping the physical exhaustion would drown out the rising tide of his own thoughts. But the silence grew heavier. Sleep became a battleground. Nightmares, fragmented and terrifying, would snatch him awake, drenched in sweat, his heart hammering. Sometimes it was the feeling of being held down, sometimes a faceless presence, always the crushing helplessness. He’d lie there, staring at the ceiling, the rhythmic breathing of Lena beside him a stark contrast to the chaos in his own head. He’d often slip out of bed, retreating to the living room couch, needing space, needing to be alone with his terror.

The world outside began to feel menacing. Up on the roof, a place he once found solace and control, now felt like an exposed stage. He’s always been meticulous about safety, but now, his hypervigilance has a new, frantic edge. Every sudden gust of wind makes him flinch. He constantly scans the ground below, not just for tools, but for any unexpected movement, any shadow that seems to linger too long. His crew notices his quietness, his quick temper when someone approaches him from behind, but they attribute it to stress or the heat. He finds it harder to focus on the precise measurements, the careful laying of shingles, his mind often drifting to that night, replaying fragments, searching for a different outcome, for a way he could have prevented it. He feels a deep, gnawing shame, a belief that he should have been stronger, should have fought back, even though he knows, logically, he was unconscious.

At home, the intimacy with Lena has dwindled to almost nothing. He stiffens at her touch, a reflex he can’t control, feeling a surge of panic and disgust at his own body. He sees the hurt in her eyes, the quiet questions, but he just pulls away further, unable to articulate the wall that has risen between them. He feels detached from his children too, struggling to connect, to laugh with them genuinely. His once-steady patience has worn thin, replaced by irritability and sudden outbursts of anger that leave him feeling even more isolated and guilty. He used to enjoy Sunday gatherings with the larger family, the communal meals and stories, but now he finds excuses to stay home, preferring the quiet, even if it’s a quiet filled with dread.

Tasi moves through his days feeling numb, an observer to his own life. The vibrant colors of the sky, the warmth of the sun on his skin – sensations he once cherished – now seem muted, distant. He feels a profound sense of hopelessness, a belief that he is fundamentally broken, that the man he was before is gone, replaced by this hollow, fearful shell. He’s exhausted, not just from the physical demands of his work, but from the constant internal battle, the struggle to keep the memories at bay, to appear normal, to keep the world from seeing the deep wound he carries. He just wants to feel safe again, to feel like himself, but the path to that seems impossibly steep, shrouded in a fog of fear and unspoken shame.
